st: An interview with Xue Lan, senior professor of humanities and social sciences at Tsinghua University
zh: 解码“中国之治” 构建中国之学
zhSub: 访清华大学文科资深教授薛澜
paras: This is an interview, published in Guangming Daily on 28 May 2026, with Xue Lan, a senior professor of humanities and social sciences at Tsinghua University who works in public administration. Reporter Zhang Sheng asks Xue to look back over the ten years since Xi Jinping's 2016 symposium on philosophy and social sciences. They ask what has changed in the field and how Chinese scholars should now build a self-reliant knowledge system.

The interview has three parts. The first reviews the policy framework since 2016 and the changes Xue sees in public administration. The second turns to the paths of knowledge, theory and method innovation, including the role of artificial intelligence. The third sets out what scholars should do next.

Xue names three changes in public administration. Research has become more autonomous. Earlier work leaned on foreign theory and used Chinese experience mainly to test it. Scholars now take major practice in reform and the modernization of national governance as the source of concepts and explanatory frameworks. Research also follows practical problems more closely, as seen in the growth of new types of think tanks, and Chinese scholars take part in international exchange with more confidence and equality. Xue argues that innovation depends on the Two Integrations: starting from Chinese realities, and drawing on traditional Chinese culture to produce original concepts and break what Xue calls the monopoly of Western-centric narratives. Xue adds that Western concepts have sometimes been applied to China without scrutiny. On AI, Xue argues that it offers new research tools and new questions, such as the lag of governance rules behind technology, and that social science must supply values and norms for its development.

Xue calls for three things: a long-term approach that avoids haste and short-term evaluation, organised and interdisciplinary research on major real-world problems such as Chinese modernization, and further work on systematising the disciplinary, academic and discourse systems. The aim is to keep scholars' subjectivity in an open environment and promote originality through mutual learning, so that Chinese ideas can offer solutions to common human problems. Read the original if you want an example of how a leading Chinese public-administration scholar describes the push for an autonomous knowledge system a decade after the 2016 symposium.
quoteEn: Scholars should hold to their own subjectivity amid openness and advance originality through mutual learning.
quoteZh: 要在开放中坚守主体性、在互鉴中推进原创性

glossary.explanation: A formulation in Party theory: integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture. Here Xue presents it as the key to innovation in the social sciences.
The official term for China's own path to modernization, promoted especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022) as distinct from Western models.

glossary.literal: new-type think tanks with Chinese characteristics
glossary.explanation: A think-tank system promoted by the Party since 2013. It is led by designated national high-end think tanks and is meant to support policy advice and theoretical innovation.

t: African scholars' perceptions and assessments of Chinese modernization
zh: 非洲学界关于中国式现代化的认知评价
paras: This article, published in World Socialism Studies (2025, no. 12), is a literature review of how scholars, think-tank researchers, commentators and political figures in Africa have assessed Chinese modernization. Wang and Lan start from the observation that Africa, the continent with the largest concentration of developing countries, has looked to China's 'development miracle' for lessons. They aim to offer an African perspective on the meaning and global contribution of Chinese modernization. Their overall finding is that most African scholars reach objective and positive conclusions, and that the research is gradually deepening.

The review is organised in three parts followed by an assessment. It first covers African views of China's achievements: the economy, governance and democracy, common prosperity, and peaceful development. It then turns to explanations of China's success, grouped under leadership, guiding ideology, the people as the main body, the political system, policy adjustment and traditional culture. The third part covers the global significance Africans attach to Chinese modernization. Most of the material is quotation from named commentators in South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Egypt, Rwanda, Zimbabwe and elsewhere.

In the authors' account, African commentators credit above all the leadership of the Communist Party of China, the Two Integrations of Marxism with Chinese realities and traditional culture, a people-centred approach, and a political system suited to national conditions. Several of them are reported to describe whole-process people's democracy as different from Western democracy. Many are said to see the Belt and Road Initiative and China's global initiatives as expanding China–Africa cooperation. The central lesson the authors draw from these voices is that 'modernization is not Westernization'. Africa should choose its own path, borrowing from China without copying it wholesale.

In their closing assessment, Wang and Lan characterise the scholarship by 'three comparisons' (past and present, China and the West, China and Africa), 'four combinations' of methods and 'three expansions' of scope. They concede that some scholars are influenced by negative opinion, and that others offer only shallow praise because the concept is recent. They argue that behind the research lies a growing African insistence on autonomy and independence in modernization. They end by quoting Xi Jinping that Africans have the greatest say on which path suits Africa, and by calling for deeper China–Africa cooperation. Read the original if you want a catalogue of African voices on Chinese modernization, as seen through a Chinese academic lens, with many named sources.
quoteEn: African scholarship is gradually trying to break free from the former mode of thinking that blindly copied so-called 'advanced experience'.
quoteZh: 非洲学界正在逐步尝试摆脱过去对于所谓“先进经验”一味照搬的思维范式

glossary.explanation: The official Party-state concept, prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022), of a socialist modernization led by the Communist Party of China. It is presented as sharing common features with other countries' modernization while reflecting China's national conditions.

An official term, promoted by Xi Jinping since 2019, for China's own model of democracy. It stresses participation across all stages of decision-making, not only elections, and is contrasted with Western electoral democracy.
A long-standing socialist goal that has been given new emphasis under Xi Jinping. It refers to prosperity shared by all, with narrower wealth gaps.
Official formulation of combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture.
China's infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative, launched in 2013, linking China with countries across Asia, Africa and Europe.

t: The modern course and scholarly character of Chinese classical studies
zh: 中国古典学研究的现代历程与学理特质
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 2 February 2026
paras: Li Zhen takes up a question raised by the recent boom in classical studies, which followed the first World Classics Congress over a year ago: what is Chinese classical studies, and what should it study? The article argues that further work needs theoretical clarification on two fronts. One is a historical account of how classical studies took shape as a modern discipline. The other is an internal understanding of the classics as the foundation of Chinese civilization. Li holds that the field's distinctive trait is its focus on canonical texts, and that the canon has repeatedly renewed itself.

The piece is a short newspaper essay in three parts. The first traces the emergence of Chinese classical studies in modern scholarship in three stages. The second asks what counts as a classic, a canonical text and a statecraft text. The third surveys changes in the canonical system from the pre-Qin period to the late Qing and after, and draws a lesson from them about civilizational renewal.

On history, Li says the term was used by Liang Qichao in 1923 for Qianlong–Jiaqing-era textual scholarship, but 'national learning' was then the more common label. It entered modern scholarship in the mid-1990s through comparative, literary-historical work centred on excavated texts of the pre-Qin and Han periods. Over the past fifteen years it has become more rooted in Chinese tradition, systematic, institutionalised and in dialogue with Western classics. Li notes that this breadth raises the question of what is not classical studies. On substance, Li argues that the field's core is the study of the fundamental principles, values, history and texts of classical China, with the canon as its main body. Citing the Zhuangzi, the Hanshu and Zhang Xuecheng, Li says the canon goes beyond Confucian classics to include the writings of the various schools of thought, as 'words that carry the Way'. Li then identifies three major shifts in the canon: its establishment in the Western Han, its reshaping in the Tang and Song, and its upheaval from the late Qing. Each shift coincided with a major turning point in history.

Li concludes that only a spirit of the age able to lead history to a higher level can become a new classic, and that the canon keeps its classic status only through continual self-renewal. Chinese classical civilization endures, Li says, because its basic principles remain open to history, not because the texts are old. Classical studies therefore looks to the classics for resources to answer the questions of the present. Read the original if you want a concise account of how Chinese scholars currently define the scope, history and purpose of Chinese classical studies.
quoteEn: Only a spirit of the age that can guide history to a higher plane can become a new classic; a new classic marks the moment when the river of civilization enters a new stretch of its course.
quoteZh: 只有能够导引历史走向更高处的时代精神才能成为新的经典，新经典是文明长河走入新航段的标志。

glossary.explanation: A modern academic field, modelled partly on Western classics, devoted to the study of China's ancient foundational texts and ideas. The article argues that the discipline emerged in the twentieth century from the modernization of traditional scholarship.
A early twentieth-century label for China's traditional scholarship as a whole. The article says it was better known than 'classical studies' in the 1920s.
Texts regarded as embodying fundamental principles and values. The article treats canonicity as the defining feature of Chinese classical studies.

t: World China studies: seeing the world from China and China from the world
zh: 世界中国学：从中国看世界，从世界看中国
paras: Li Bozhong, writing in Guangming Daily, argues that the study of China has become a worldwide field, which he calls "world China studies" (Global China Studies). The newspaper commentary holds that this field should be built on a two-way perspective: seeing the world from China and China from the world.

The article first traces how research on China developed. It moves from the Chinese "national learning" (guoxue) and Western "Sinology", both centred on classical texts, to the "new Sinology" and to Marxist studies of China. It then covers postwar "Chinese Studies" in the United States, Europe and Japan, which turned to contemporary China and to the social sciences. The second half sets out the method of two-way verification, cites Chinese and foreign voices in support, and ends with institutional milestones.

Li contends that Sinology and guoxue studied "China in the texts" and said little about present-day China, while Chinese Studies took "real China" as its object. In his account, the international debate on the "Great Divergence", set off by the California School and Kenneth Pomeranz's 2000 book, moved Chinese history to the centre of global scholarship and shows that world China studies now belongs to the academic mainstream. He argues that internal and external views each have limits, citing Su Shi, Wang Guowei, Zhou Youguang, Seymour Martin Lipset, Kerry Brown and Martin Jacques. Only combining them, he says, gives a full picture. Citing Charles Tilly, he adds that China's pre-modern path can serve as a yardstick for other regions, which shows that world development has several models.

Li holds that Chinese scholars, with the richest resources and the largest research community, should play the main role, while the field stays open to scholars of every country. He points to Dunhuang studies, where Chinese scholars moved to the front after reform and opening up. He cites the 2004 World China Studies Forum, the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences institute set up in 2012, the World China Studies Conference since 2023, and programmes at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and other universities. He concludes that China is well placed to build a centre of world China studies. Read the original if you want a concise, officially oriented account of how Chinese scholars frame the history and future of China studies as a global field.
quoteEn: Without entering inside, how can one grasp the details; without stepping outside, how can one recognise the form.
quoteZh: 不入乎其内，焉得其细节；不出乎其外，焉识其形态。

glossary.explanation: A term that emerged in the late Qing and early Republican period for China's own traditional scholarship, centred on the classics, history, philosophy and belles-lettres. It was coined in contrast to imported Western learning.
The Western academic study of traditional Chinese civilisation, begun in Europe in the 16th century and based on philology and classical texts.
A term advanced by the World China Studies Forum from 2004, with the English name Global China Studies. It denotes China research conducted worldwide by scholars in China and abroad.
The debate on why Europe industrialised ahead of China and other regions. Kenneth Pomeranz's 2000 book and the California School gave it prominence.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in China from 1978.

t: Understanding China and understanding the world: the two-way convergence of world China studies and area studies
zh: 读懂中国与理解世界：世界中国学与区域国别学的双向奔赴
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 29 October 2025
paras: Writing in a newspaper commentary, Li Kaisheng asks how area and country studies (regional and country studies, qū yù guóbié xué) relate to world China studies, meaning the study of China by scholars abroad. Li argues that the two fields share a mission, which is to understand a heterogeneous "other", and should therefore learn from and cooperate with each other.

The piece first contrasts area studies with international relations. In Li's account, international relations studies the interaction between states, while area studies examines why a given region or country differs from others, at both international and domestic levels. Li then sets out three methodological dimensions for understanding another country: historical time, environmental space and the internal system.

Li compares the international relations view of states to billiard balls that follow mechanical rules, and the area studies view to team sports in which each player's skill and will matter. On this basis Li calls world China studies "the area studies of other countries". Li criticises Western "democracy export" as a failure to respect other countries' conditions. The three dimensions are illustrated with cases: US tariff policy as a sign of hegemonic decline; the claim that India is the "next China", which Li says ignores a changed international environment; and Chinese innovation, which Li attributes to a combination of factors rather than to state subsidies.

Li concludes that China's development dynamics are still poorly understood abroad, and that China needs to grasp profound changes in other countries if its policy initiatives are to take root. Li presents mutual understanding as key to world peace and development at a time of national rejuvenation, and calls the cooperation of the two fields urgent. Read the original if you want a short, officially aligned statement of how Chinese scholars position area studies and overseas China studies together.
quoteEn: World China studies is in fact the area studies of other countries; both share a common mission, which is to study the particularity of other countries, and both are studies of national conditions and distinctive features.
quoteZh: 世界中国学其实就是世界其他国家的区域国别学，两者都有一个共同的使命，那就是对其他国家的特殊性进行研究，都是国情之学、特色之学。

glossary.explanation: A field in China devoted to the in-depth study of particular regions and countries, including their history, culture, politics and society. It was formally established as a first-level discipline in China in 2022.
The study of China conducted by scholars and institutions outside China, treated in China as a field of research in its own right.
A central goal in Chinese Party discourse, usually rendered officially as the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Here it is used to describe China's current stage of development.

t: China's journey back to the world stage
zh: 中国重返世界舞台的历程
paras: This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks how China has returned to a central position in world affairs and what its global vision offers. The author, an Egyptian political scientist, argues that China's rise rests on a long historical experience and that its proposals deserve attention because they answer pressing needs of a troubled international order.

The piece moves from China's image as a peaceful civilisation to its transformation from a colonised, divided country into the second-largest economy. It then turns to the period since 2013, the Belt and Road Initiative, and the Global Development, Security, Civilization and Governance Initiatives. The last of these was put forward by Xi Jinping at the "SCO Plus" meeting in Tianjin.

Said contends that China's conduct cannot be understood without the "century of humiliation" and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, two themes that shape its self-image. Since 2013, the author says, China has pursued the status of a core world power on three pillars: national revival, a community with a shared future for mankind, and more Chinese wisdom in global governance. The Belt and Road Initiative is presented as a new, more open and balanced model of globalisation, open to states of any political system and tilted towards developing countries. Said adds that this vision is gaining recognition in the Global South.

Said concludes that the old order can no longer meet common human challenges, and that scholars, policymakers and ordinary people must understand China's past, present and future to grasp their own shared future. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a young Arab scholar presents China's global role in a Chinese state-affiliated outlet.
quoteEn: Without considering these ideas, which form the basis of China's understanding of itself and of the world, China's actions cannot be understood.
quoteZh: 若不考量这些形成中国自我认知与世界认知基础的理念，便无法理解中国的各项举措。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2013, calling for multilateral cooperation and shared security and development.
An infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative launched by China in 2013, linking Asia, Africa and Europe.
A term for developing countries, often used in Chinese diplomacy to describe China's partners.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A Party slogan for restoring China's national strength and international standing after the "century of humiliation".
A historical narrative about China's subjection to foreign powers from the mid-19th to the mid-20th century, central to Chinese national identity.

t: Historical and contemporary China in a global perspective
zh: 全球视野下的历史中国与当代中国
paras: In this short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, the British writer Martin Jacques argues that the role, nature and importance of China studies are being transformed in step with China's own rise. His thesis is that China studies has become a global phenomenon, and that its main obstacle is a paradigm gap between China and the West.

Jacques compares the field today with that of twenty years ago, when study of China was concentrated on China itself and pursued mainly by sinologists. He then covers the field's geographical shift towards the Global South, the effect of social media and artificial intelligence, and the Western habit of judging China by Western standards.

Jacques contends that as China becomes central to global growth, climate change, governance, technology and the Global South, China studies grows more interdisciplinary and of interest to non-specialists. He argues that the field's centre of gravity is moving away from the West: countries such as Brazil, Nigeria, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia need to understand China through the Belt and Road Initiative, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and trade, and they increasingly form views from their own experience. For Jacques, most Western scholars still view China through a Western prism and measure it by its degree of 'Westernisation', so that China always 'fails'. He attributes this to two centuries of Western hegemony and a single-world-view mentality, which he says leaves Western predictions about China almost always wrong.

Jacques concludes that China studies is only at the beginning of a major expansion, and that China's history, culture, governance and foreign policy remain largely misunderstood. He holds that China must be understood on its own terms, and that the demand for such understanding will be the field's chief challenge in coming decades. Read the original if you want a brief, openly polemical statement of how a prominent Western commentator on China sees the globalisation of China studies and the decline of Western interpretive authority.
quoteEn: China is not the West; it never was, and it never will be.
quoteZh: 中国不是西方，从前不是，也永远不会是。

glossary.explanation: A term for developing countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America, used in Chinese official discourse to stress solidarity and shared development interests with China.
An infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative launched by Xi Jinping in 2013, linking China with countries across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.

t: Entering China's vast contexts to expand China Studies
zh: 深入博大中国场景 拓展中国学研究
paras: Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2025, around the second World Conference on China Studies, Lin Shangli asks how China Studies should develop as it becomes an international field. Lin's answer is that any account of China detached from Chinese contexts risks becoming spectating from the far shore. Research should therefore be embedded in three settings: a continuous civilisation of five thousand years, a super-large-scale society, and socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The short commentary takes these three settings in turn, calling them the temporal, spatial and ecological scenes of China Studies. It opens by citing Xi Jinping's letter to the first World Conference on China Studies, which described the field as the study of both historical and contemporary China. It closes with a call for China Studies to move beyond studying China as an object.

In Lin's account, the temporal scene means treating ancient language, philosophy and culture as continuous with contemporary development. The spatial scene rests on what Lin calls the "Chinese miracle": rapid economic growth, long-term stability and effective governance. Lin cites a population of over 1.4 billion, GDP above 130 trillion yuan, 660,000 urban and rural communities and a five-level chain of decision-making as a "large-sample laboratory" for economics, political science and policy studies. The ecological scene is the "living experience" of socialism with Chinese characteristics, including Party leadership, the people's congress system and consultative democracy. Lin links these to traditional governance logics and says they can test the limits of existing theories and yield new analytical frameworks.

Lin concludes that a new form of human civilisation is the concentrated expression of Chinese civilisation, society and socialism, not an abstract concept. China Studies should move from "object study" to "joint theory-building", engaging with concepts such as whole-process people's democracy, Chinese modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a leading university president frames the agenda of China Studies.
quoteEn: Only by embedding research in the three settings of a continuous five-thousand-year civilisation, a super-large-scale society and socialism with Chinese characteristics can we produce Chinese knowledge that truly understands and explains China and benefits humanity.
quoteZh: 唯有把研究嵌入五千年连续文明、超大规模社会与中国特色社会主义这三重场景，才能产出真正读懂中国、解释中国、造福人类的中国知识。

glossary.explanation: A comprehensive field studying China's history, culture, society and economy. In recent Chinese usage it is promoted as an international field, with World Conferences on China Studies held since 2023.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's path of socialist development since reform and opening up.
An official concept, promoted since 2019, describing China's democratic system as covering all stages of political and policy processes.
The official term for China's own path of modernization, presented by the Party as distinct from Western models.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and global-governance concept advanced by Xi Jinping, stressing common interests and joint development.

t: Drawing a new pattern of peace and prosperity through the Global Governance Initiative: an interview with Kyrgyzstan's former prime minister Djoomart Otorbaev
zh: 以全球治理倡议绘就和平繁荣新格局——访吉尔吉斯斯坦前总理卓奥马尔特·奥托尔巴耶夫
paras: This is an interview, conducted by Chu Guofei of Chinese Social Sciences Today, with Djoomart Otorbaev, former prime minister of Kyrgyzstan. It followed the "Global Strategic Dialogue (2025)" held on 28 October 2025 at the Institute of History of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, on the 80th anniversary of the United Nations and the new pattern of global governance, where Otorbaev gave an opening address. He argues that the UN should be reformed rather than abolished, and that China's Global Governance Initiative is timely and significant.

The questions move through four themes: the UN's role and its biggest challenges; the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) as a model of efficient multilateralism; China–Kyrgyzstan cooperation and inclusive economic globalisation; and the role of academia in global governance. Along the way Otorbaev discusses the Belt and Road Initiative, ASEAN, BRICS and the position of the Global South.

Otorbaev says the UN's membership has grown from 51 to 193 states and its "content" has changed since 1945, so ideas for improving it are urgently needed. He describes the SCO, which in his account has grown from six members to a 26-country "family", as a model because its documents rest on consensus; he praises the Tianjin summit of 2025 and says Kyrgyzstan will chair the SCO in 2026, with a summit in Bishkek. In his view China's initiative rests on respect for sovereignty, non-violence and mutual benefit, and the SCO resists development models imposed on Eurasia. He says Central Asia's five states endorse the initiative. He criticises protectionism by the United States and the European Union, which he says have lost competitiveness, and presents the Global South as committed to free trade and investment.

Otorbaev points to the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway as a flagship Belt and Road project, stresses trust as the precondition for cooperation (citing Confucius), and says equal dialogue requires education and knowledge. He describes BRICS as a Global South mechanism not directed against the West, and says scholars must help lead the world towards greater prosperity. Read the original if you want a Central Asian former head of government's view of China's Global Governance Initiative, the SCO and Global South cooperation.
quoteEn: We have always held that the peaceful and efficient development of multilateral institutions is the only path to building a fairer world.
quoteZh: 我们始终认为，多边机构的和平、高效发展，是构建更公平世界的唯一途径。

glossary.explanation: A proposal presented by China at the SCO Tianjin summit in 2025. It calls on states to work together towards a more just and reasonable global governance system, with equal participation by all countries.
A term for developing and emerging countries, widely used in Chinese official discourse to describe states that China presents as partners in reforming the international order.
A Eurasian political, security and economic organisation founded in 2001, with China, Russia and Central Asian states among its members.
China's infrastructure and connectivity programme launched in 2013, linking China with Eurasia, Africa and beyond through investment in transport and trade projects.

t: The value of the Digital Silk Road for win-win cooperation
zh: 数字丝绸之路对合作共赢的价值
paras: Ivan Sharafanov, a foreign faculty member at the University of International Business and Economics, asks what the Digital Silk Road contributes to international cooperation and how its obstacles might be overcome. This commentary, originally published in Economic Daily on 24 October 2025, argues that the initiative is a practical response to the current stage of technological change. In the author's view, it upgrades the Belt and Road Initiative's connectivity model, offers a platform for coordinating multilateral rules, and serves as a public good for global digital economic cooperation.

The article begins with Xi Jinping's proposal of the concept at the first Belt and Road Forum in 2017 and his follow-up remarks in 2019. It then moves through three sections: the rationale for building the Digital Silk Road, practical cooperation in two fields, and policy responses to current problems. The author cites figures on digital economy growth, including a Chinese digital economy of 53.9 trillion yuan in 2023, and examples such as the China–Pakistan cross-border optical cable, the China–ASEAN Information Harbour, the 'Silk Road e-commerce' framework and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP).

Sharafanov's central claim is that the Digital Silk Road extends 'hard connectivity' (energy, ports, railways) into 'soft connectivity' in cloud computing, big data, 5G, artificial intelligence, cross-border cables and the alignment of digital rules and standards. He contrasts rising trade protectionism in some countries with China's promotion of open cooperation, secure cross-border data flows and compatible technical standards. He identifies obstacles: fragmented global digital governance, hard multilateral coordination, new digital trade barriers, data security and privacy concerns, and limited voice for emerging economies in standard-setting.

The author proposes three measures: stronger bilateral and multilateral rule coordination, using the WTO, RCEP and the G20 and creating regional digital trade demonstration zones; a dispute-settlement mechanism for digital trade, drawing on WTO experience; and closer cooperation on data security and privacy, with basic compatibility of standards while respecting national data sovereignty. He concludes that the initiative gives emerging economies more say in global digital governance and gives fresh momentum to global recovery and sustainable development. Read the original if you want an example of how a foreign academic in China presents the Digital Silk Road in the official policy framing, with the cited statistics and examples.
quoteEn: The Digital Silk Road is not only an organic combination of digital economy development and the joint building of the Belt and Road, but also an important public good for advancing global digital economic cooperation.
quoteZh: 数字丝绸之路不仅是数字经济发展与共建“一带一路”的有机结合，更是推动全球数字经济合作的重要公共产品。

glossary.explanation: A component of the Belt and Road Initiative covering digital infrastructure, digital trade and technology cooperation. Xi Jinping first used the term at the 2017 Belt and Road Forum.
China's international cooperation initiative launched by Xi Jinping in 2013, focused on infrastructure, trade and connectivity across Asia, Europe, Africa and beyond.

glossary.zh: 区域全面经济伙伴关系协定
glossary.pinyin: Qūyù Quánmiàn Jīngjì Huǒbàn Guānxì Xiédìng
glossary.explanation: A free trade agreement among Asia-Pacific countries, including China and ASEAN members, with a chapter on e-commerce.

t: A Spaniard's observations on Chinese modernization
zh: 一个西班牙人对中国式现代化的观察
paras: Julio Ceballos, a Spanish business consultant and writer, contributed this piece to the People's Daily to accompany his Spanish-language book Xuanji Tu (the Xuanji Diagram). The book draws on 18 years of work and life in China. Ceballos argues that China is not an unsolvable puzzle but a living jigsaw, and that its development experience offers lessons for Europe. The thesis is that there is no single fixed recipe for modernization: each civilisation can find its own path.

The text is a first-person commentary built around four themes: why he wrote the book, strategic patience, education and innovation, and resilience and solidarity. It rests on anecdotes from Sichuan, Shandong, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Nanjing and Jinan, together with a few figures on research spending and talent. The book's title refers to an ancient astronomical instrument and to a palindrome poem by Su Hui, which he reads as a sign that there are many ways to meet global challenges.

Ceballos's central contrast is between European political horizons, limited by election cycles and quarterly reports, and Chinese planning over decades, carried by the Five-Year Plans. In his account this continuity is sustained by a cadre promotion system based on experience, results and execution, which he calls performance-oriented governance. He also holds that China treats education, digital strategy and AI ethics governance as long-term national investments, and that social cohesion works as a ready-made resource when crises arrive. He cites figures that China leads the world in high-level scientific talent and in total research personnel, and that its 2024 R&D spending exceeded the EU average.

Ceballos presents his book as an invitation and a bridge between Europe and China, not as uncritical praise or an idealised comparison. He admits that no system removes all problems. He proposes cooperation on resilience, social cohesion and community collaboration, with mutual respect for difference. His closing formula is "one equation, many solutions". Read the original if you want an example of how a foreign business observer's praise of Chinese long-term planning is presented in the Party's flagship newspaper, as one of the China Studies pieces on this site.
quoteEn: One equation, many solutions. China's experience tells us that modernization has no fixed recipe: each civilisation can build on its own distinctiveness and irreplaceable strengths and, through an organic fusion of political governance, universal education, innovation-driven growth, social cohesion and spiritual values, find the development path that suits it.
quoteZh: 一个方程，多种解法。中国的经验告诉我们：现代化没有固定配方，每一种文明都可立足自身的独特性与不可替代的优势，在政治治理、教育普及、创新驱动、社会凝聚与精神价值的有机融合中，探索出适合自身的发展道路。

glossary.explanation: China's medium-term national development blueprints, issued since 1953, setting economic and social goals for each five-year period. Ceballos treats them as the institutional carrier of long-term continuity.

Ceballos's own label for a cadre system in which officials are promoted on the basis of demonstrated results and experience across several posts. He links it to the traditional idea of appointing the capable.

t: Filling the gap in global narratives of the Second World War
st: Interview with Ivona Ladjevac, deputy director of the Institute of International Politics and Economics, Serbia
zh: 填补全球二战史叙事空白——访塞尔维亚国际政治经济研究所副所长伊沃娜·拉杰瓦茨
paras: This is an interview, published in Chinese Social Sciences Today on 29 September 2025, with Ivona Ladjevac, deputy director of the Institute of International Politics and Economics in Serbia. The reporter, Wang Youran, spoke to her after the launch of the English edition of A New History of the Second World War, edited by the Institute of World History at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. The launch and an international conference, "Rebirth from the Fire: Civilization and War", took place in Athens on 28 August.

The interview has three questions: what Ladjevac took from the event, how the book differs from mainstream Western histories, and what its multilingual publication means for reflection on the war and for peace. The book is already on sale in Greece and the United States, and further language editions are being prepared.

Ladjevac argues that the book draws on primary sources in Chinese, English, German, Japanese, French and Russian, including material from China and other non-Western theatres that Western accounts under-use. She stresses its position that the war began with the 18 September 1931 Incident, not with Germany's invasion of Poland in 1939, which makes China's resistance the first major front against fascism and the main Eastern theatre. In her view, placing East Asia at the centre changes readers' picture of the war and balances world historical narrative, which matters at a time when, she says, many try to alter history.

Ladjevac concludes that the English edition lets Chinese scholarship reach global readers across a language barrier and encourages comparative reflection. She says this "mutual visibility" would make global memory of the war more balanced rather than uniform. She also holds that the book's account of solidarity against aggression carries lessons for a world of geopolitical tension. Read the original if you want a Serbian scholar's endorsement of the Chinese claim that the war began in 1931, or a view of how this Chinese-edited history is being received abroad.
quoteEn: By placing East Asia and China at the centre rather than the margins, the book changes the historical picture in many readers' minds and lets them understand the Second World War from multiple fronts on a more equal footing.
quoteZh: 通过将东亚和中国置于中心而非边缘，该书改变了许多读者心中的历史图景，使他们能够更加平等地从多条战线理解二战。

glossary.explanation: The 1931 Japanese seizure of Shenyang and then north-eastern China (Manchuria), after an explosion on the Mukden railway. Chinese historiography treats it as the start of the war of resistance against Japan.

keywords: A New History of the Second World War

t: Promoting open research cooperation and linking China with the world: an interview with Magdalena Skipper, Editor-in-Chief of Nature
zh: 共促科研开放合作，联结中国与世界——访《自然》总编辑玛格达莱娜·斯基珀
paras: This is an interview, published in Guangming Daily on 25 September 2025, in which reporter Yang Yifu speaks with Magdalena Skipper, Editor-in-Chief of Nature and Chief Editorial Advisor for the Nature Portfolio. It took place in Beijing as Springer Nature set up a China Academic Advisory Council and held its first forum. The article's framing is that Chinese research is advancing rapidly and that publishers are paying closer attention to cooperation with Chinese scientists. Skipper's main message is that China is making major progress across many fields and that open, trustworthy science depends on broad collaboration.

The interview has four sections. The first covers why the council was created and how it is composed. The second deals with the history of Springer Nature's cooperation with China and Skipper's view of Chinese research. The third turns to open and credible science, including open data and transparent peer review. The fourth addresses the challenges and uses of artificial intelligence in research and publishing.

Skipper says the council is a platform for exchange among the parts of the research ecosystem. It has 25 leaders from research, funding, policymaking and industry, rotating every three years, and it includes early-career researchers and women scientists. It follows similar councils established since 2021 in the United States, Europe, Africa and Latin America. She points to the Nature Index 2024 research leaders ranking, where China stays first, and says Chinese work is moving from internationally driven projects to independent domestic development. She attributes this to state funding and years of overseas training and joint research. On openness, she stresses data sharing with fair credit for data generators, privacy protection and the UNESCO principle of "as open as possible, as closed as necessary". She also describes Nature's decision, from 16 June 2025, to publish peer review reports with accepted original research articles.

On AI, Skipper says it cannot be an author because it cannot take responsibility, that AI used as a research tool beyond simple copy-editing must be declared, and that Springer Nature uses AI tools to detect misconduct such as image manipulation. She expects China's progress to strengthen and calls for cooperation across disciplines, sectors and countries. Read the original if you want a publisher's view of China's place in global science, Nature's transparency policies and its AI rules, as presented in a Chinese state newspaper.
quoteEn: Research is in fact a social, human endeavour, and it flourishes when there is collaboration.
quoteZh: “科研实际上是一项社会性的人类事业，当存在合作时，才会蓬勃发展。

t: The junzi (exemplary person) in Chinese culture
paras: Wang Xuedian asks what the figure of the junzi, often rendered "gentleman" or "exemplary person", contributes to Chinese culture, and argues that no other type so fully embodies the Chinese nation's moral ideals and pursuit of personality. In Wang's account, the concept moved from an aristocratic title under the kinship-based Zhou order to a personal ideal open to all. The article, a newspaper essay drawn from a longer book chapter, holds that understanding junzi culture is a way to grasp the mainstream of Chinese culture itself.

The essay proceeds in five parts. It traces the term's history from the Book of Documents and Book of Songs through Confucius, Mencius and Xunzi. It then examines the junzi's image, using jade, the "four gentlemen" of plum, orchid, bamboo and chrysanthemum, and the "nine virtues". Next it considers the junzi's essence and the means of self-cultivation. It then describes how the ideal permeated society, and ends with its modern forms.

Wang's central claim is that the core quality of the junzi is ren (benevolence). Figures such as Qu Yuan and Su Dongpo, whose conduct departed from the classical descriptions, were still widely called junzi because of their humane concern. On cultivation, Wang follows the Great Learning: sincerity of intent and rectifying the heart are the route of self-cultivation, ideally extending outward to family, society and the world. The ideal spread through Han-dynasty Confucian primacy and the Tang–Song examination system, which, Wang says, carried it from the court into village life and shaped national character.

Wang notes Liang Qichao's 1914 Tsinghua lecture, which compared the junzi with the English gentleman and urged adapting the ideal to a new age. Contemporary junzi, in Wang's examples, include the rice scientist Yuan Longping and border guards, and the modern ideal is open equally to all. Wang calls for creative transformation and innovative development of fine traditional Chinese culture, and for cultivating modern junzi personality as the core of an "ethics-oriented" Eastern way of life. Read the original if you want a concise, officially published overview of how a leading Chinese scholar presents the junzi tradition and its contemporary uses.
quoteEn: The core quality of the junzi personality in Chinese culture should be "ren" (benevolence).
quoteZh: 中国文化中君子人格的核心品质应当是“仁”。

glossary.explanation: A central Confucian term for the morally exemplary person. It originally denoted aristocratic status and was recast by Confucius as a moral ideal.
Benevolence or humaneness, the supreme Confucian virtue, centred on caring for others by extending one's own feelings to them.
An official phrase for the parts of China's cultural heritage that Party and state documents regard as worth inheriting and promoting.

glossary.zh: 创造性转化、创新性发展
glossary.explanation: An official formula for adapting traditional culture to contemporary needs rather than simply reviving it.

t: The cultural-strategic significance of building the China Studies Literature Research Centre at the National Library of China
zh: 国家图书馆中国学文献研究中心建设的文化战略意义 ·
source: Chinese Journal of Library Science, 2025, vol. 51, no. 4
paras: Chen Ying asks what role the China Studies Literature Research Centre of the National Library of China should play in the strategy of building a socialist cultural power. China studies is defined as research by overseas scholars, including ethnic Chinese abroad, who read China through the eyes of an "other". It covers traditional sinology, studies of modern China and the tracking of current political, economic and social questions. The article, published in the Chinese Journal of Library Science in 2025, argues that the Centre's collections, reference tools, policy services and exchange work all serve that strategy, and that it should be rebuilt around digital and intelligent methods.

The article first sketches the history of China studies abroad and of Chinese scholars' attention to it. It then traces the National Library's collecting since the 1920s: the foundations laid under Yuan Tongli, exchange networks after 1949, and later purchases. It reports holdings as of the end of 2024 of more than 150,000 titles in over 90 languages, more than 200 foreign periodicals and six purchased databases. Next it reviews three kinds of output: bibliographies, the journal International Sinology, and other studies. It then covers policy-reference services and cultural exchange, and ends with weaknesses and proposed remedies.

Chen's central claim is that the Centre should be positioned as "one repository and three centres": a general China studies repository, an academic research centre, a decision-reference centre and a cultural exchange centre. The author argues that the strategy of becoming a cultural power, set out at the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020) and the 20th Party Congress (2022), gives libraries their mission: preserving Chinese civilisation, supporting cultural innovation, guiding public culture and promoting exchange and mutual learning. The author lists gaps, including thin coverage of Latin America and Africa, scarce manuscripts, outdated reference works, limited AI use, shortage of translators and a lack of any joint catalogue. Proposed responses are systematic acquisition, a "smart" collecting system, faster updates of reference works, a handbook series on China studies in each country, knowledge-graph databases, machine translation, a global union catalogue and training in Chinese cataloguing.

Chen concludes that the Centre, guided by the cultural-power strategy and renewed through digital technology, should become a window for the state and the public on world trends and a foundation for taking Chinese culture abroad. The author presents it as belonging to both China and the world. Read the original if you want a detailed institutional history of China studies collecting in China's national library, or want to see how a library professional ties this work to Party cultural policy and to policy-advisory functions.
quoteEn: The China Studies Literature Research Centre of the National Library belongs to China and also to the world, and it will surely become a cornerstone for Chinese culture going global and a temple of culture that China studies scholars worldwide aspire to.
quoteZh: 国家图书馆中国学文献研究中心是中国的,也是世界的,她必将成为中华文化走向世界的基石,成为全世界中国学学者向往的文化殿堂。

glossary.explanation: Research on China by overseas scholars, including traditional sinology and the study of contemporary China. Xi Jinping described it in 2023 as both the study of historical China and of contemporary China.
A national goal set out at the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020) and in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), aiming to build a strong culture by 2035.
The Centre's stated positioning: a general China studies repository plus academic research, decision-reference and cultural exchange centres.

t: The Global Development Initiative in the perspective of world Sinology: motives, impact and prospects
zh: 世界中国学视域下的全球发展倡议：动因、影响与前景
paras: Gao Xiaosheng and Du Yaning ask how foreign governments, think tanks, media and scholars have read the Global Development Initiative, which Xi Jinping first proposed at the UN General Assembly on 21 September 2021. The authors say existing Chinese research explains the initiative mainly from China's own standpoint and rarely examines overseas perceptions with primary sources. Working from the perspective of world Sinology, they set out to analyse the initiative's 'mirror image of the other'. They conclude that international responses are broad, practical and mostly positive, though they contain some misreadings.

The article is organised around three questions, each answered through overseas sources. It first reviews why, in outsiders' view, China launched the initiative. It then covers the initiative's impact at national, regional and global levels, and its prospects, including challenges and potential. The authors draw on institutions and figures such as the Asia Foundation, ISEAS, AidData, the Lowy Institute, the Atlantic Council, the European Parliament's foreign affairs committee, and scholars and officials from Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas.

On motives, the authors report three overseas readings: a response to China's internal and external development pressures; a diplomatic move to widen China's influence at the UN and in global governance; and a step towards changing the international order, seen variously as raising the Global South's standing, as geopolitical rivalry, or as a push for a fairer order. On impact, they say foreign commentators see the initiative as helping to deliver the UN 2030 Agenda, as a platform for cooperation and experience-sharing, and as breaking the monopoly of a Western-centred model such as the 'Washington Consensus'. On prospects, overseas observers cite vague mechanisms, domestic pressures in China, an unclear relation to the Belt and Road Initiative, economic uncertainty, geopolitical suspicion and competition from other donors.

The authors identify three features of the overseas response: comprehensive and varied perspectives, a pragmatic orientation towards implementation and national interest, and generally positive views mixed with misreadings. They attribute the misreadings to political stance, class perspective and Cold War thinking, for example politicising development or treating the initiative as a tool of rivalry with the United States. They conclude that the initiative has moved from concept to practice, and call for a measured, dialectical reading of foreign views and for steps to guide more accurate international understanding. This, they argue, would support a more inclusive Chinese discourse and the image of a responsible major power. Read the original if you want a dense, source-rich survey of how foreign think tanks and scholars have interpreted the Global Development Initiative, as reported by Chinese researchers.
quoteEn: The Global Development Initiative has moved from conceptual construction into a stage of deepening practice, and its results depend not only on China's own efforts and promotion but even more on recognition and support from the international community.
quoteZh: 全球发展倡议已从理念构建迈入实践深耕阶段，其实施成效不仅取决于中国自身的努力和推动，更需要国际社会的认可和支持。

glossary.explanation: A framework Xi Jinping announced at the UN General Assembly in September 2021. It stresses development as a priority, people-centred growth, inclusiveness, innovation, harmony with nature and action-orientation, and is linked to the UN 2030 Agenda.
The study of China by scholars and institutions outside China, which Chinese academics increasingly treat as a source for understanding how China is perceived abroad.
A term for developing countries, mostly in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Chinese official discourse uses it to frame China's solidarity and cooperation with them.

China's infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative, launched in 2013. The article notes that overseas observers debate whether the Global Development Initiative runs parallel to it, replaces it or complements it.

A set of market-oriented policy prescriptions, such as trade and financial liberalisation, promoted for developing economies from the 1990s. Chinese commentary often contrasts it with China's own development path.

t: The moral dilemma of the Ming loyalists
paras: This piece, published in the journal Guoxue in February 2014 and credited to Wei Fedi (Frederic Wakeman), asks how the men who had served the Ming dynasty coped morally and intellectually with its fall in 1644 and with their own survival under the Qing. The author argues that guilt, scholarship and a new historical relativism shaped the loyalists' response, and that the Qing eventually absorbed their loyalty into its own legitimacy.

The text moves from individual cases to intellectual history and then to state policy. It opens with the poet Wu Weiye, who served the Qing and was burdened by guilt, and goes on to the painter Chen Hongshou and the historian Zhang Dai, who changed their names or their way of life. It then turns to the philosophers Huang Zongxi and Wang Fuzhi, to the decline of Wang Yangming's idea of innate moral knowledge, and to the Kangxi, Shunzhi and Qianlong emperors' treatment of the loyalists.

The author first argues that many loyalists turned to poetry and above all to history-writing, both to commemorate 1644 and to bury it. Kangxi's special examination of 1679 and the invitation to help compile the official Ming History, in the author's reading, gave them a shared stake with Chinese officials who had submitted to the Qing. Second, loyalists faced an uncomfortable question: Donglin idealism had fed factional strife, while Chinese collaborators were carrying out the fiscal, legal and economic reforms the late Ming literati had wanted. This pushed thinkers such as Wang Fuzhi towards a functionalist, historically relative view in which institutions and moral judgements depend on their particular period and set of relations.

Wakeman holds that this relativism did not last. A broad reaction against Wang Yangming's school and the revival of Cheng-Zhu orthodoxy, backed by Kangxi and others, brought back absolute duties such as loyalty and filial piety. Qing rulers, ambivalent towards anti-Manchu loyalists, praised their loyalty as an abstract virtue; honours rose under Shunzhi and Kangxi and peaked under Qianlong, who was motivated largely by anger at the turncoat Qian Qianyi. By the time of the 1673 Revolt of the Three Feudatories, loyalty to the Qing had overtaken loyalty to the Ming. Read the original if you want a compact account of how early Qing intellectuals and rulers reshaped the memory of Ming loyalism.
quoteEn: In short, the Ming loyalists' pursuit of a distant moral goal produced confusion in the politics of the present.
quoteZh: 简言之,明朝忠臣对遥远的道义目标的追求导致了眼前政治的混乱。
